summaryEn: Hoya explores Janggyeong Panjeon, the 15th-century halls at Haeinsa whose clever windows and layered floors have protected the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks for some 500 years.
learningGoalsEn: Know that Janggyeong Panjeon at Haeinsa Temple was built to store the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks and dates from the 15th century.
Understand two design features that protect the woodblocks: windows of different sizes for airflow, and a floor layered with charcoal, lime, salt and sand to control moisture.
Know that Janggyeong Panjeon was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1995.
Read and recognize 건물 (geonmul), 창문 (changmun), 숯 (sut), 바람 (baram) and 지켜요 (jikyeoyo).

origin.noteEn: Heritage history, researched from the sources listed on the Sources screen.

keywords.en: Janggyeong Panjeon, the woodblock storage halls at Haeinsa
Joseon, the Korean dynasty of that time

scenes.narrationEn: Hoya visits Haeinsa Temple and climbs to the highest part of the temple grounds. Here stand the Janggyeong Panjeon, the halls made to store the woodblocks. They are the oldest buildings still standing at Haeinsa.

keyword.en: Janggyeong Panjeon, the woodblock storage halls at Haeinsa

scenes.artBrief: Hoya climbing stone stairs to a terrace at the top of a mountain temple; two long, plain wooden halls with tiled roofs stand side by side above the other temple roofs.

art.altEn: Hoya climbs to the highest part of Haeinsa, where the two long halls of Janggyeong Panjeon, its oldest buildings, stand.

scenes.captionEn: The oldest halls still standing at Haeinsa

scenes.narrationEn: Two long halls stand side by side: Sudarajang in the south and Beopbojeon in the north. Two small buildings sit at the ends, so together they form a rectangle around a courtyard.
scenes.artBrief: Bird's-eye view of four plain wooden buildings forming a rectangle around a sandy courtyard, two long and two short; Hoya waves from the courtyard.

art.altEn: Seen from above, two long halls and two small ones form a rectangle around a courtyard, where Hoya waves.

scenes.narrationEn: These halls were built in the 15th century, during the Joseon dynasty. There are no fancy decorations. Every part was designed for one job: keeping the woodblocks safe.

keyword.en: Joseon, the Korean dynasty of that time

scenes.artBrief: Front view of a long, simple wooden hall with unpainted pillars and rows of slatted windows; Hoya points out how plain and tidy it looks.

art.altEn: A long, plain wooden hall from the 15th century: no fancy decoration, every part made to keep the woodblocks safe.

scenes.captionEn: Plain halls built for one job

scenes.narrationEn: Look at the windows! The windows on the front and back walls are different sizes, and the upper and lower windows differ too. This helps the wind flow through the halls.
scenes.artBrief: Cutaway side view of a hall: slatted windows of different sizes high and low on opposite walls, with gentle curved arrows of breeze flowing through past the shelves; Hoya's fur ruffles in the wind.

art.altEn: A cutaway hall shows windows of different sizes, high and low on its two walls, letting a breeze flow past the shelves.

scenes.narrationEn: Now look down. Under the earthen floor are layers of charcoal, lime and salt with sand. They soak up extra moisture when the air is damp and give it back when it is dry.
scenes.artBrief: Cross-section of the ground under a hall showing simple colored layers (black charcoal, white lime, pale salt, tan sand) beneath an earthen floor; Hoya kneels, peering at the layers.

art.altEn: Under the earthen floor lie layers of charcoal, lime and salt with sand, soaking up damp and giving it back when the air is dry.

scenes.captionEn: Charcoal, lime and salt under the floor

scenes.narrationEn: Wind, sunlight and earth work together. Thanks to this natural design, the woodblocks have stayed safe from damp, mice and insects for some 500 years.
scenes.artBrief: Sunlight streaming through slatted windows onto rows of woodblocks; a small mouse and a beetle turn away outside the wall while a breeze swirls leaves; Hoya smiles.

art.altEn: Sunlight and a gentle breeze keep the woodblocks dry and safe from damp, mice and insects, and Hoya smiles.

scenes.captionEn: Wind, sun and earth keep blocks safe

scenes.narrationEn: In 1995, UNESCO added Janggyeong Panjeon to the World Heritage List. UNESCO says it is the oldest storehouse of the Tripitaka, the Buddhist scriptures.
scenes.artBrief: The two long halls under a clear autumn sky with colorful maple leaves on the mountain; a soft glowing outline around the buildings suggests special recognition. No logos or text.

art.altEn: The two long halls stand under a clear autumn sky among maple trees: Janggyeong Panjeon is on the World Heritage List.

scenes.narrationEn: To help keep the temperature and dampness inside steady, visitor entry is limited. Hoya peeks through the window slats and whispers, "Uriga jikyeoyo, we protect it!"
scenes.artBrief: Hoya and a child quietly peeking through vertical window slats from outside, careful not to touch; inside, shelves of woodblocks rest in calm shadow.

art.altEn: Hoya and a child peek through the slatted windows from outside without touching, because entry is limited to protect the blocks.

scenes.captionEn: Entry is limited to keep the air steady

facts.claimEn: Janggyeong Panjeon are the buildings at Haeinsa built to store the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks. They stand at the highest part of the temple grounds, above the hall of the main Buddha.

facts.claimEn: Two long buildings, each 15 bays wide, stand side by side: Sudarajang to the south and Beopbojeon to the north. With two small buildings at the east and west, they form a rectangle around a courtyard.
facts.claimKo: 정면 15칸의 긴 건물 두 동이 남북으로 나란히 서 있는데, 남쪽은 수다라장, 북쪽은 법보전이며, 동·서쪽의 작은 건물 두 동과 함께 긴 네모꼴로 배치되어 있다.

facts.claimEn: The depositories date from the 15th century (early Joseon). The date of first construction is unknown; rebuilding is recorded in 1488. They were built simply, without decoration, to serve their purpose.
facts.claimKo: 장경판전은 15세기(조선 전기) 건물로, 처음 지은 연대는 정확히 알 수 없으나 1488년에 다시 지은 기록이 있으며, 장식 없이 간결하게 지었다.

sources.title: Haeinsa Temple Janggyeong Panjeon, the Depositories for the Tripitaka Koreana Woodblocks
sources.quoteOrLocator: "Constructed in the 15th century in the traditional style of the early Joseon period, their design is characterized by its simplicity of detailing" [text re-read on an Internet Archive snapshot of this UNESCO page; the live page blocks automated requests]

sources.title: 국보 합천 해인사 장경판전 (陜川 海印寺 藏經板殿) — 국가유산 상세 정보 및 국가유산 설명
sources.quoteOrLocator: "처음 지은 연대는 정확히 알지 못하지만 … 성종 19년(1488)에 학조대사가 왕실의 후원으로 다시 지어 '보안당'이라고 했다는 기록이 있다."; "장식 요소는 두지 않았으며"

sources.title: 합천 해인사 장경판전 — 한국민족문화대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: "'弘治元年(홍치원년)'이라는 각명(刻名)으로 건립연대를 1488년(성종 19)으로 추정하고 있다."

facts.claimEn: For ventilation, the windows differ in size between the south and north (front and back) walls, and the upper and lower windows also differ in size.
facts.claimKo: 통풍을 위해 앞뒤(남북) 벽의 창 크기를 서로 다르게 하고, 위아래 창의 크기도 달리하였다.

sources.title: 국보 합천 해인사 장경판전 (陜川 海印寺 藏經板殿) — 국가유산 상세 정보 및 국가유산 설명
sources.quoteOrLocator: "통풍을 위하여 창의 크기를 남쪽과 북쪽을 서로 다르게 하고 각 칸마다 창을 내었다." / EN: "Each depository has two rows of windows in different sizes -- one on the front and the other on the rear -- designed to ensure effective natural ventilation."

sources.title: 유네스코 등재유산 소개 — 세계유산 「해인사 장경판전」

sources.title: Haeinsa Temple Janggyeong Panjeon, the Depositories for the Tripitaka Koreana Woodblocks
sources.quoteOrLocator: "They were specially designed to provide natural ventilation and to modulate temperature and humidity" [text re-read on an Internet Archive snapshot of this UNESCO page; the live page blocks automated requests]

facts.claimEn: Beneath the earthen floor are layers of charcoal, lime and salt laid with sand, which help regulate humidity by absorbing excess moisture and releasing it when the air is dry.
facts.claimKo: 흙바닥 속에 숯, 횟가루(석회), 소금을 모래와 함께 차례로 넣어 습도를 조절하도록 하였다. 습기가 많으면 빨아들이고 건조하면 내뿜는다.

sources.title: 국보 합천 해인사 장경판전 (陜川 海印寺 藏經板殿) — 국가유산 상세 정보 및 국가유산 설명
sources.quoteOrLocator: "안쪽 흙바닥 속에 숯과 횟가루, 소금을 모래와 함께 차례로 넣음으로써 습도를 조절하도록 하였다." / EN: "The earthen floor is laid over layers of powdered charcoal, lime, salt, and sand"

sources.title: 유네스코 등재유산 소개 — 세계유산 「해인사 장경판전」
sources.quoteOrLocator: 영상 해설: "많은 양의 숯과 소금 석회를 이용해 기초를 다졌다. 이로써 과도한 습기는 흡수하고 건조 할 때는 머금었던 습기를 내뿜어 항상 일정한 습도를 유지하게 했다."

facts.claimEn: Because the design makes use of natural conditions (sunlight, ventilation, and control of temperature and humidity), the woodblocks have been preserved for some 500 years, safe from rodents and insects.
facts.claimKo: 햇빛과 환기, 온습도 조절 등 자연환경을 이용한 설계 덕분에 경판이 약 500년 동안 쥐나 벌레의 피해 없이 보존되었다.

sources.title: Haeinsa Temple Janggyeong Panjeon, the Depositories for the Tripitaka Koreana Woodblocks
sources.quoteOrLocator: "adapted to climatic conditions, thus preserving the woodblocks for some 500 years from rodent and insect infestation" [text re-read on an Internet Archive snapshot of this UNESCO page; the live page blocks automated requests]

sources.title: 유네스코 등재유산 소개 — 세계유산 「해인사 장경판전」
sources.quoteOrLocator: "건물 내의 환기, 온습도 조절 등 자연 기상에 적응하도록 설계되어 500년 간 깨끗하고 안전하게 경판을 보존할 수 있었음."; 영상 해설: "햇살을 충분히 받아 나무가 눅눅해지거나 썩는 일이 없다."

facts.claimEn: Haeinsa Temple Janggyeong Panjeon was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1995, and UNESCO describes it as the oldest depository of the Tripitaka.
facts.claimKo: 해인사 장경판전은 1995년 유네스코 세계유산에 등재되었으며, 유네스코는 이를 가장 오래된 대장경 보관 건물로 평가한다.

sources.title: Haeinsa Temple Janggyeong Panjeon, the Depositories for the Tripitaka Koreana Woodblocks
sources.quoteOrLocator: "Date of Inscription: 1995"; "As the oldest depository of the Tripitaka, they reveal an astonishing mastery of the invention and implementation of the conservation techniques" [text re-read on an Internet Archive snapshot of this UNESCO page; the live page blocks automated requests]

sources.quoteOrLocator: "합천 해인사 장경판전은 15세기 건축물로서 세계 유일의 대장경판 보관용 건물이며, 1995년 12월 유네스코 세계문화유산으로 등재되었다."

facts.claimEn: UNESCO says visitor entry into the Janggyeong Panjeon is restricted so that the temperature and humidity inside the depositories can be controlled. Since June 2021 Haeinsa has also offered a small, pre-booked guided tour inside Beopbojeon (10 to 20 people per session), so entry is limited rather than impossible.
facts.claimKo: 유네스코는 장경판전 안의 온도와 습도를 조절하기 위해 방문객의 출입을 제한하고 있다고 밝히고 있다. 해인사는 2021년 6월부터 법보전 내부를 사전 예약자(회당 10~20명)에 한해 안내 탐방하고 있어, 출입은 '제한'될 뿐 전면 금지는 아니다.

[text re-read on an Internet Archive snapshot of this UNESCO page; the live page blocks automated requests]

verification.notes: Third independent pass. Every cited URL for all 6 episodes (52 facts) was re-opened (UNESCO pages via Wayback copies when the live site resets connections) and quotes/locators were compared; the one exception is unesco.org/en/prizes/literacy (unreachable from here; its claim is now also backed by a Korean MCST press release). Eight minimal corrections were made: (1) Hangeul Day f3 no longer says 'Gregorian' (no cited source says the October 9 conversion was Gregorian; encykorea separates Julian/Gregorian only for 1932-45) and dates the October 29/28 observances; (2) f10 gains a third source (SBS 2018 with 국립한글박물관 curator); (3) Shapes scene 8, learning goal and f7 now say 'South Korea's spelling rules' count 24 (North Korea counts 40, 국립한글박물관 webzine 59); (4) Sejong scene 4/f4: 백성 is 'an old-fashioned word' with 표준국어대사전 added; (5) Jikji f8 quote no longer repeats a prize amount that differs between UNESCO page versions; (6) Tripitaka f6 wood and corner plates now have two further sources (정책브리핑; 박상진 wood-identification study); (8) Hangeul Day f9 gains a second source (문화체육관광부 press release); (7) Panjeon scene 8/f9: 'visitors cannot walk inside' replaced by 'visitor entry is restricted' because Haeinsa has run pre-booked tours inside Beopbojeon since June 2021. See hangul-printing.signoff.md.

authorNotes: Theme is set to 'crafts' because the episode is about building and conservation design; switch it to 'letters' if the cluster should stay in one theme. The original construction date is unknown (국가유산포털), so the narration says '15th century' (UNESCO WHC, 국가유산포털). The sources consulted do not say which wall or row has the larger windows, so the narration only says the sizes differ, and illustrations should not suggest a specific pattern. 국가유산포털 also calls it the 'world's only building for storing Tripitaka woodblocks'; the narration uses UNESCO's more conservative wording, 'oldest depository of the Tripitaka', instead. The building's survival through the 1592 war is left out, because the story avoids war content. The visitor-entry restriction is as stated on the WHC page on the access date; rules may change.
